title: Perineal Injuries in Obstetrics and Surgery
subject: Surgery
summary: Perineal trauma occurs during childbirth, trauma, or surgery and can lead to pain, infection, and functional loss. Recognising the type of injury, assessing severity, and initiating appropriate management are essential, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: A perineal injury is a disruption of the skin, muscle, or mucosa of the perineum, often graded from I to IV based on depth and structures involved.
b: Grade I: superficial skin only
Grade II: skin + perineal muscles, no anal sphincter
Grade III: involves external anal sphincter (IIIa) or both external and internal sphincter (IIIb)
Grade IV: extends through the rectal mucosa

sections.p: Obstetric perineal tears are staged I‑IV; surgical lacerations are described by depth and involvement of sphincter or rectal mucosa.
b: Staging guides repair technique and need for specialist input
Higher grades carry higher risk of infection, incontinence, and chronic pain

sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals the most common causes are:
b: Instrumental vaginal delivery (forceps, vacuum)
Prolonged second stage of labour
Large fetal head or macrosomia
Maternal factors: primiparity, episiotomy, rigid perineum, malnutrition

sections.p: Patients report perineal pain, bleeding, and difficulty with voiding or defecation after delivery or trauma.
b: Visible laceration or hematoma
Blood at the urethral meatus suggests urethral injury
“Butterfly” perineal hematoma may extend into scrotum or lower abdomen

t.a: Visual inspection and gentle digital rectal exam
t.b: Confirms grade and sphincter involvement; avoids further trauma
Detects occult sphincter defects when visual exam is equivocal
Looks for hematuria indicating urethral injury

t.a: If ultrasound unavailable, perform a gentle probe exam under local anaesthetic
t.b: Provides bedside assessment of sphincter integrity

sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening or cause long‑term disability.
b: Urethral or rectal perforation → urine/ fecal contamination
Infection leading to abscess or sepsis
Persistent incontinence after repair

sections.p: Repair should be performed promptly, preferably within 6 hours, using a step‑wise approach.
b: Analgesia and prophylactic antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin‑gentamicin) to prevent infection
Grade I‑II: simple interrupted sutures of skin and muscle (absorbable polyglactin)
Grade III‑IV: layered repair – muscle, external sphincter, internal sphincter, mucosa; consider senior surgical input
Avoid episiotomy unless absolutely indicated (foetal distress, rigid perineum)
If a large hematoma is present, evacuate and pack; give iron if anaemic
Review wound at 48 h and again at 2 weeks for infection or dehiscence
Pelvic floor physiotherapy for grades III‑IV to improve continence
Teach proper perineal hygiene and warm sitz baths
Preventive measures: controlled second stage, judicious use of episiotomy, adequate maternal nutrition
Perineal hematoma without laceration – managed conservatively unless expanding
Anal fissure – superficial mucosal tear, not involving sphincter
Rectovaginal fistula – chronic communication, not acute tear

sections.p: Certain findings may give a false sense of security.
b: Absence of visible skin tear does not exclude deep sphincter injury; always perform a gentle rectal exam
Normal urine dipstick does not rule out urethral injury if blood is microscopic; consider catheterisation with gentle technique

whenToSeekHelp: Severe perineal bleeding causing tachycardia or hypotension
Suspected urethral or rectal perforation with urine/feces in the wound

faq.q: What is the difference between a grade II and grade III tear?
faq.a: Grade II involves skin and perineal muscles only; grade III also involves the external anal sphincter (IIIa) or both external and internal sphincter (IIIb).
Only for clear obstetric indications such as fetal distress, instrumental delivery, or a rigid perineum that threatens severe tearing.

faq.q: How do I recognise a urethral injury?
faq.a: Look for blood at the meatus, inability to pass urine, and a high‑dripping urine stream; confirm with gentle catheterisation if needed.

exam: A primigravida presents 2 hours after a forceps delivery with a painful perineal laceration and blood at the urethral meatus — what immediate steps do you take? — Assess bleeding, perform a gentle urethral catheterisation, give prophylactic antibiotics, and plan repair; if catheterisation fails suspect urethral injury and refer.

During a vaginal delivery you notice a ‘butterfly’ perineal hematoma extending into the scrotum — how does this change your management? — Evacuate the hematoma, pack the space, give IV fluids and antibiotics, and monitor for expanding bleed; avoid tight dressings.

A patient with a grade III perineal tear complains of fecal leakage after repair — what are the likely causes and next actions? — Incomplete sphincter repair or infection; perform a bedside ultrasound or endoanal exam, consider re‑exploration, and start stool softeners and pelvic floor physiotherapy.

In a low‑resource clinic you lack perineal ultrasound; how can you still assess sphincter integrity? — Perform a careful digital rectal exam under local anaesthetic, looking for a defect or loss of tone; document findings and arrange referral if uncertain.

Why is routine episiotomy discouraged in modern obstetric practice? — It increases risk of higher‑grade tears, infection, and postpartum pain without reducing maternal or fetal morbidity when not indicated.

A woman presents with a perineal tear after a home delivery attended by a traditional birth attendant; what infection‑prevention measures are essential? — Clean the wound with sterile saline, give a single‑dose broad‑spectrum antibiotic (e.g., ampicillin‑gentamicin), and arrange follow‑up for wound inspection.

What are the key components of a layered repair for a grade IV tear? — Separate and close the rectal mucosa, internal sphincter, external sphincter, and perineal skin using absorbable sutures, ensuring tension‑free approximation.

A patient develops a fever 48 h after perineal repair; what complications should you consider? — Surgical site infection, abscess formation, or necrotizing fasciitis; obtain wound cultures, start empiric antibiotics, and consider drainage if fluctuant.
